title: Joining, carefully
hookLine: joining a tradition is serious, and each has its own way in: the Buddha tells an eager new follower to slow down
tomorrow: what does Athens have to do with Jerusalem?

cards: Plenty of apps beg you to sign up: a pop-up, a discount, one tap and you're in. The Buddhist suttas keep an odd scene.

Upali, a rich householder and a devoted follower of another teacher, the Jain leader Nataputta, goes to the Buddha to win a debate. He loses, gladly, and asks to become the Buddha's follower on the spot.
And the Buddha, of all people, tells him to slow down.

teach.b: In substance he says: make a careful investigation; that's good for a well-known man like you. Upali is even more pleased. Another teacher, he says, would have paraded my name through town on banners.
He asks again, and the Buddha adds something stranger: your house has long supported the Jain monks, so keep giving to them when they come. Why would a teacher slow down his own new follower?
Because in this tradition, joining is serious and has a shape.
A person becomes a Buddhist lay follower by going for refuge: to the Buddha, to the Dhamma, his teaching, and to the Sangha, the community. It's said aloud, and it's meant.
A rushed yes after one good debate isn't the same thing. And the word about the Jain monks shows the other side: joining one community is no excuse to slight the people who fed you before.
And Upali goes for refuge a third time, eyes open.

teach.h: EACH TRADITION KEEPS ITS OWN DOOR.
teach.b: Each tradition keeps its own door. In Christianity, it's baptism. In Islam, bearing witness with the shahada.
Sikhs who take initiation receive amrit. Converting to Judaism goes through a rabbinic court.

teach.h: ASK THE PEOPLE WHO KEEP IT.
teach.b: Each is serious, and each is kept by its own people. So the way in isn't found on a website. You ask them.

how: A Buddhist lay follower goes for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, usually before a teacher or community; other traditions have their own rites of entry, kept by their own people. A newcomer asks a member or teacher how joining works there.

o: signing up after one good visit, the faster the better
becoming part of a tradition through its own door, carefully

games.q: after one inspiring retreat, your cousin wants to quit her church choir and drop her friends there to join the retreat's community tomorrow. by the Upali Sutta, what would the Buddha say?
o: look carefully first, and keep honoring the people who fed you.
join tomorrow; a feeling that strong is the sign it's right.
never join anything; stay free of every community.
games.why: the Buddha told Upali to investigate carefully, and to keep giving to the Jain monks his house had long supported.

practice: Think of one person who belongs to a tradition you're curious about. Version a short message asking how a person joins, and what they wish newcomers knew.
Get the words right, then set the phone face down and rest with the question.

wordCard.voice: Joining: becoming part of a tradition through its own door, carefully. In Buddhism, that door is going for refuge.

orig.note: Pali: I go to the Buddha for refuge, the first of the three refuges.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: ask them, and listen when they tell you to slow down. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 56, Upali Sutta (Upali, follower of Nigantha Nataputta, comes to debate; asks to become a lay follower; 'make a careful investigation'; other sects would carry banners; keep giving alms to the Niganthas; he goes for refuge)
Khuddakapatha 1, Saranagamana (the three refuges: Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Dhammaṃ…, Saṅghaṃ…)
